title: RAG is Not Dead: Josef's Sam Flynn on Legal Tech That Works
author: Sam Flynn

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source supports the narrower premise that subject-matter expertise helps lawyers assess whether AI output is moving in the right direction. st.t: Continuous learning: Filtering matters more than release chasing
st.an: Flynn directly accepts the cluster’s emphasis on delivering practical value rather than chasing successive releases. He materially extends it by identifying sound handling of legal knowledge sources—including document structure and hierarchy—as a prerequisite for useful legal AI, while relying on experiential examples rather than measured performance evidence.

st.t: Expertise pipeline: Automated work weakens succession routes
st.an: Flynn accepts the cluster’s broader view that AI reshapes legal-service delivery rather than merely replacing lawyers, and materially develops its institutional-knowledge theme: useful self-service depends on correctly structured, reliable knowledge sources and can release lawyers for strategic work. He does not directly address apprenticeship, associate leverage or partner succession, so his contribution extends the implementation model rather than substantiating the cluster’s central pipeline risk.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Flynn accepts the cluster’s core case for selective, expert-governed deployment and materially extends it with a concrete closed-domain architecture: maintained organisational knowledge, pre-launch expert validation, and post-launch controls and escalation. He is more bullish about bounded non-expert self-service, but conditions it on reliability and safe removal of experts rather than general autonomy.
qs: If you don’t get the knowledge source right, all of that is going to be for naught.
You want to build in controls, triggers, escalation pathways, feedback loops.

st.t: AI procurement: Product expansion exceeds realized value
st.an: The source supports shifting attention from product proliferation and hype to the conditions that produce practical legal-AI value. Its inventory evidence measures expanding product coverage rather than adoption or returns, while Flynn argues that value depends on sound knowledge sources and expert involvement. It does not, however, provide measured deployment or economic outcomes.

st.t: Civil justice: Capacity gains need human safeguards
st.an: Flynn directly supports the cluster’s human-safeguard proposition: legal AI should retain human intervention, with expert validation before deployment and monitoring afterward. The source describes a concrete oversight model but does not establish quantified safety, accuracy or access-to-justice capacity gains.
qs: So it’s not about getting humans out of the workflow.
And then post-launch, you have workflows, triggers, access to data that helps you track performance of the tool as well.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Flynn supports the value of specialist legal workflow software through self-service document automation and AI Q&A, linking it to faster transactions and greater strategic capacity. His evidence is anecdotal rather than comparative, and some business-facing tools operate without lawyer interaction, so the source is less firmly aligned with the cluster’s predominantly verified-copilot framing.

st.t: Legal workflows: Contextual agents remain lawyer-guided
st.an: The source supports the lawyer-guided aspect of the cluster: Lambert reports that AI is most useful in domains where lawyers already have expertise because they can judge whether it is proceeding appropriately. Flynn’s broader claims of transformation and increased attention are personal and anecdotal, so they do not materially extend the cluster’s workflow, integration or implementation case.

st.t: Meaningful access: AI uptake cannot close justice gaps
st.an: Flynn supports the proposition that AI can expand meaningful legal help: he says legal-aid tools can be deployed with suitable implementation support and can answer questions that previously never reached attorneys. His account also implies that uptake requires partners, tools and regulatory change, but it supplies no independent evidence that deployment produces sustained access-to-justice gains or closes the justice gap.

st.an: The source broadly supports the proposition by characterising generative AI as transformative while presenting its strongest practical benefit as expert-led use by lawyers who can assess whether outputs are sound. kp.k: Legal AI product counts indicate rapid market expansion
kp.d: Stephanie Wilkins reports that Legal Tech Hub's map, published March 3 using research through February 19, contained 400 generative-AI products in 17 categories; an update two weeks later exceeded 500 across 18 categories, partly following requests for inclusion. Leading categories were broad legal assistants, contracts and litigation. Nikki Shaver interprets this as making adoption inevitable and recommends AI strategies and policies; her expectation of a thousand solutions a year later is a prediction, not an observed count.
qs: And at the time it showed 400 different legal tech products using generative AI across 17 broad categories.
And in that two weeks, had then over 500 solutions across 18 broad categories.
I’ve gone out on a limb and said that I believe a year from now we’ll have a thousand solutions with generative AI.

kp.k: Reliable knowledge retrieval remains foundational to advanced workflows
kp.d: Flynn argues that RAG and workflows are complementary rather than competing approaches: sophisticated systems still depend on correctly structured source knowledge. He contrasts generic tools that split clauses or ignore document hierarchy with Josef's reported two years of work across thousands of legal and compliance documents, involving research partners at NYU and Cornell and customers including L’Oreal and Orrick.

kp.d: Flynn reports an unnamed developer's claim that value-delivering agentic workflows operating in legal and compliance could be counted on one hand. This is secondhand testimony, not a systematic market measurement. He attributes some attention to innovation theater and engagement incentives, while acknowledging substantial technological opportunities and urging practical implementation of existing capabilities.

kp.k: Model changes require continuing safety and maintenance checks
kp.d: Flynn believes major foundational-model leaps have ended and describes recent advances as changes in interaction with underlying technology. That is his assessment, not a demonstrated finding. Despite suggesting reduced effects on application development, he warns that even small model changes can fundamentally alter outputs, requiring strong maintenance and safety checks in enterprise and high-risk legal deployments.
qs: I think we’ve seen the end of the great leaps in the foundational layers.
But every tweak in the underlying model can fundamentally change the way that the output is created or generated.
then you need to have very solid safety and maintenance checks in place to make sure that the answers and the outputs are still coming out in the way that you want it to.

kp.k: Self-service shifts routine work away from corporate lawyers
kp.d: Flynn carries a customer GC's anecdotal claim of not seeing a sales contract for six months, compared with several complex contracts daily previously. He says self-service generation now takes seconds for simple agreements or minutes for complex ones, freeing the GC for strategic work and reducing sales-team waits. He also describes L’Oreal document automation, Bupa business-facing Q&A without lawyer interaction covering insurance regulations and HR policies, and Bumble privacy tools, including possible future consumer-facing applications.
qs: I haven’t seen a sales contract in six months.
And he used to see several every day if they got too complex.
that answer questions for the business without any lawyer interaction on topics as complex as private health insurance regulations through to HR and people policies.

kp.k: Tenant self-service depends on maintained sources and expert verification
kp.d: Discussing Roxanne with Housing Court Answers and NYU, Flynn describes Josef as a closed-domain system using existing organizational knowledge, including tenancy explainers already maintained by the organizations. Experts test actual tenant questions before launch and validate or change answers; post-launch workflows, triggers and performance data retain human oversight. His account presents these as reliability mechanisms, without reporting numerical accuracy or error results.

That information is already being kept up to date and complete.
They feed them into the tool, they get the answer, and they validate it. Yes, no, change it, right?

kp.k: Nonexpert tools require selective escalation, not complete expert removal
kp.d: In response to Lambert's concern about nonexperts recognizing errors, Flynn distinguishes Josef's client- and public-facing ambition from expert copilots such as Harvey. He describes pre-launch expert verification through a reliability assessment framework presented at Stanford and Maastricht University, followed by controls, escalation pathways and feedback loops. Invoking Megan Ma's self-driving-car analogy, he emphasizes knowing when humans should take over rather than pursuing complete automation.
qs: We need this tool to be reliable enough to give responses to non-experts, which many people thought was a crazy thing to do.
You want to build in controls, triggers, escalation pathways, feedback loops.
So it’s definitely not about removing the experts completely from the loop. It’s about removing the experts from the loop where you can safely.

kp.k: Automation could scale assistance and enable strategic advocacy
kp.d: Lambert reports Sateesh's potential capacity increases of 10, 100 or 1,000 times; Flynn explains the mechanism as teaching a system to answer questions from a knowledge base so it can repeat assistance at scale, subject to computing and distribution. These are potential scale effects rather than measured Roxanne outcomes. Flynn also argues that usage data can help legal-aid organizations improve resources and identify recurring tenant problems for strategic advocacy.

kp.k: Automated answers may expand demand for expert intervention
kp.d: Flynn acknowledges displacement anxiety when routine questions consume substantial expert time, citing unspecified research that answering questions occupies 30 % of an expert's day. He argues from his experience that self-service expands lawyers' and compliance officers' total addressable market by engaging people who previously ignored policies. Question patterns could expose bullying or data breaches and redirect professionals toward proactive interventions and executive reporting. His illustrative policy-engagement figures of five to ten percent are not accompanied by study details.

launching these tools actually increases the TAM for lawyers and compliance officers.

kp.k: Bias governance combines knowledge, training, rules and accountability
kp.d: Flynn analogizes AI governance to managing human behavior: supply appropriate knowledge, train over time, establish behavioral rules and moderate unacceptable outputs. On privacy, he asserts that the additional issue beyond existing contract-management or intake-tool considerations is whether data is stored in the model, particularly for training or fine-tuning. His reassurance about confirming non-storage is explicitly his opinion, not a demonstrated privacy assessment.
qs: So knowledge, education, rules. You set rules for what the tool can and can’t do.
And then finally, you have a layer of accountability.
But if you can confirm with whoever you’re working with that the data isn’t stored in the model, then in my humble opinion, you’re good to go.

kp.k: Expert copilots can produce knowledge for public-facing tools
kp.d: Flynn describes a complementary relationship between expert and nonexpert applications. Internal copilots can handle more complex, higher-risk material while expert use generates validated question-and-answer pairs that he argues can subsequently support safer nonexpert access. He also recounts housing lawyers discovering unfamiliar resources while testing Roxanne, suggesting tools can challenge even experts' assumptions about what they know.
qs: you can have an internal copilot that is trained on much more complex, high risk data for the experts.
I think as experts, we get very comfortable and we stop questioning what we know.
you’re actually creating a data set that can safely be surfaced to non-experts because you’re creating validated Q and A pairs, which is perfect fodder for an LLM.

kp.k: Legal-aid expansion combines replication with regulatory acceptance
kp.d: Flynn reports that Cornell and the Ithaca Tenants Union's tool is ready to launch, with projects about to begin in Michigan and Pennsylvania and potentially Tennessee. He says a year of learning has reduced development from conception to launch-ready tools to a couple of weeks. He views US regulatory change and bar acceptance as important, arguing that these services meet previously unserved questions rather than take existing attorney work; this is his market-expansion claim, not measured displacement evidence.

We’ve now, we can now go from conception of an idea to launch ready tool in a couple of weeks.

kp.d: Flynn predicts an unrecognizable workplace within three years and argues meaningful transformation is already technically possible. He identifies expert buy-in as the main challenge: trusted systems need people who understand content, clients and context. He warns that nonexperts already consume AI-generated legal information, potentially from the wrong jurisdiction, and frames professional participation as the condition for positive rather than harmful change.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Sam Flynn argues that grounded AI self-service can automate routine legal work, expand access to legal knowledge, and redirect experts toward strategic work, provided that experts build and supervise reliable systems.
pts.d: Flynn says RAG remains important because sophisticated workflows still depend on correctly structured knowledge sources. He believes major foundational-model leaps have ended and changes increasingly concern how underlying technology is used, while acknowledging that model tweaks can change outputs. He describes self-service contracting and Q&A as reducing legal-team bottlenecks and enabling non-experts to obtain answers without routine lawyer interaction. He argues that automated answers can scale legal-aid capacity and expand the total addressable market for lawyers and compliance professionals by reaching previously unserved questions. He also says question data can support proactive compliance work and strategic tenant advocacy. He distinguishes expert copilots from Josef's ambition to support direct non-expert use: experts remain involved in validation and escalation, rather than checking every answer. He further argues that expert use can generate validated Q&A pairs suitable for non-expert applications. Looking ahead, he predicts an unrecognizable workplace within three years and says substantial transformation is already possible with existing technology.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: Flynn principally supports his claims with product-development experience, customer examples, project experience, and unspecified research, rather than reported quantitative evaluations.
pts.d: For RAG and reliability, Flynn cites two years of development across thousands of legal and compliance documents with customers and research partners including NYU and Cornell. For self-service, he reports a Bay Area health-tech customer's experience of removing sales contracts from the GC's routine workload; this is a customer anecdote relayed by Flynn, not an independently measured result. He also identifies L’Oreal document automation, Bupa business-facing Q&A, and Bumble privacy tools as applications. He cites research that answering questions occupies 30% of an expert's day but supplies no study identification or methodology. His market-expansion claim is explicitly grounded in his experience. For safe deployment, he describes a reliability assessment framework presented at Stanford and Maastricht University, expert verification of real tenant questions, and post-launch controls, without supplying accuracy scores or comparative test results. His account of housing lawyers discovering unfamiliar resources at a Fordham conference is anecdotal. The thousand-answers-per-day example illustrates an automation scaling argument, not a reported deployment measurement. His skepticism about widespread value-producing agentic workflows includes an unnamed practitioner’s account; that secondhand count is not established as Flynn's own market measurement. The three-year workplace forecast is his stated belief, not a quantified forecast.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Flynn presents useful automation as available now, rapid legal-aid deployment as achievable with the right support, and broader workplace transformation as a three-year prospect; reliability and expert participation are conditions throughout.
pts.d: At the time of the 2025 interview, Flynn describes two years spent improving document grounding and non-expert reliability. He says a year of learning on legal-aid projects now permits movement from an idea to a launch-ready tool in a couple of weeks, conditional on having the right partner and tool. He describes Cornell and the Ithaca Tenants Union as ready to launch, projects in Michigan and Pennsylvania as about to begin, and Tennessee as a possibility. His scaling argument is explicitly subject to computing capacity and distribution. Reliable use depends on trusted, maintained source material, expert verification before launch, and monitoring, triggers, escalation pathways, and feedback after launch. He cautions that underlying-model changes can alter outputs and require safety and maintenance checks in enterprise and high-risk settings. He says more complex agentic workflows introduce additional variables that make validation harder. He presents expert buy-in and regulatory change as important to wider adoption. His privacy position is that, beyond existing software privacy and data-control considerations, users should confirm that their data is not stored in the model; this is presented as his opinion, not as a demonstrated guarantee.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are in-house lawyers and compliance teams, business users, legal-aid organizations, tenants, and other non-experts seeking legal help.
pts.d: Flynn says in-house counsel can spend less time on routine contracts and questions and more time providing strategic value. Sales teams gain faster agreement generation, while business users gain easier access to policy and regulatory information. Compliance professionals can use patterns in questions to identify risks and intervene proactively. These are enterprise workflow benefits, distinct from his access-to-justice claims. For legal aid, he says self-service can extend assistance to tenants and others whose questions previously did not reach attorneys, while enabling providers to improve resources and pursue advocacy using demand data. He acknowledges that removing question-answering tasks can feel threatening to professionals but frames the outcome as market expansion and role redirection rather than a quantified reduction in jobs. Experts gain assistance and discovery of overlooked knowledge while retaining responsibility for system construction, verification, and escalation. Non-experts gain direct access but face risks from wrong answers or jurisdictionally inappropriate information; Flynn argues that legal experts must participate because the public already uses general-purpose AI for such questions.
